newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Phillips warns of inflation danger.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Phillips warns of inflation danger.

text.p: Growing wage pressures in the economy may signal a higher potential for inflation, Federal Reserve governor Susan Phillips warned Thursday.

While Phillips said higher wages had not yet fuelled higher inflation, she hinted that the central bank was watching the economy closely for any sign of overheating and was ready for a pre-emptive strike if needed.

"We certainly are seeing pressures in certain areas and I do think that (with) as tight a labour market as we have, that is a foreboding sign in terms of the potential for inflationary increases," she said in an interview.

Fed policy-makers are to meet Aug. 19 to consider their next move on interest rates. They last raised short-term rates on March 25, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation. They have held rates steady since.
"I think that the economy is doing really quite well so one is always trying to look (at) what kinds of things could go wrong," Phillips said.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan told lawmakers two weeks ago the central bank would raise rates if needed to head off inflation, but suggested that might not happen any time soon.
Phillips said the economy been strong the past two quarters, but that a slight slowdown in growth had given inflation fighters some breathing room.
"It (was) comforting to see. That provided some relief," she said of the slowdown. The current expansion is the third longest in the United States since World War II.
According to government statistics, the economy grew at a 2.2 percent pace in the April-June period, down from a hefty 4.9 percent in the first quarter of the year.
Meanwhile, inflation remains subdued. Wholesale prices have fallen for a record six months and consumer prices so far this year have risen at the slowest pace since 1986.
Phillips noted that if businesses could continue to offset higher wage pressures with increased productivity, inflation was likely to remain muted.
"Certainly we have to pay a good deal of attention to productivity," she said, adding that so far both productivity and corporate earnings seemed to be "holding up."
With labour markets tight and new workers hard to find, businesses may try to pass on higher wage costs to customers by raising prices, fuelling inflation.
The Labour Department said last week that the jobless rate fell to a 25-year low of 4.8 percent in July and the economy created a stronger-than-expected 316,000 jobs.
Phillips said the strong jobs data made it likely that growth would pick up somewhat in the third quarter. "We'll see a bit stronger (growth)," she said, but declined to give a specific number.

The central banker added the dollar's current strength reflected the good performance of the U.S. economy. "The economic situation is pretty strong here, so the currency is probably reflective of that," she said.
